seoTitle: Add Custom HTML to Squarespace Easily
metaDescription: Add a Code block to a Squarespace page for HTML and CSS on any plan, and see why a pasted <script> tag needs the Core plan or higher to actually run.
intro: Squarespace's built-in tools cover a lot, but sometimes you need a custom element, a styled button, a script, an embedded widget, that only custom HTML provides. Squarespace doesn't bury this behind a developer mode; it's a Code block, sitting in the same content panel as every other block type you already drag onto a page. This guide covers where that block lives, what its editor looks like, how to tell whether your HTML is actually rendering before you save, and the one plan restriction that trips people up.
prerequisites: Basic comfort reading HTML and CSS, since the Code block is a plain text editor with no visual assistance
An existing Squarespace site with a page you're able to edit
costNote: HTML, Markdown, and CSS inside a Code block work on every Squarespace plan, including the entry-level Basic tier. Running JavaScript inside a Code block, or using site-wide code injection, needs the Core plan or higher; paste a <script> tag on Basic and it sits there inert with nothing to show for it.

steps.heading: Open the page you want to edit
steps.body: From the site dashboard, the sidebar lists Website, expandable into Pages, Styles, Assets, and SEO/AIO, alongside Products & Services, Content & Memberships, Scheduling, and more further down. Selecting Website and then a page like Home drops you into a live preview with an EDIT button top left; the page header confirms its status, for example "Home — Page · Published," so you always know whether you're changing something already live.

image.caption: The Website editor open on the Home page, with Pages, Styles, Assets, and SEO/AIO listed under Website in the left sidebar, and the live page preview on the right.

steps.heading: Find the Code block in the content panel
steps.body: Click Edit, then the plus icon to insert a new block, and a categorized panel slides open. Under a Code heading near the top sit three options side by side: Code, Markdown, and Embed. Code is for raw HTML and CSS, Markdown for lightly formatted text, Embed for pasting a URL or third-party snippet instead of writing markup yourself. Below that, the same panel lists Links (Social Links, Search Field, Page Link, Tag Cloud, RSS, Archive) and Integrations (Instagram, Tock, SoundCloud, Flickr). A lot of what people reach for custom HTML to build already has a native block here, and the native version usually themes better with the rest of the site.

image.caption: The block-insert panel with Code, Markdown, and Embed options under a Code heading, plus Links and Integrations sections listing native alternatives like Social Links and Instagram.

steps.heading: Write or paste your HTML into the Code block
steps.body: Dropping a Code block onto the page opens a Content panel with a Mode dropdown set to HTML and a Display Source Code toggle. The editor is a plain text area where you write markup and CSS together: one example defines two button classes with background colors set by hex code (#04AA6D for green, #008CBA for blue), styling properties like border-radius, padding, and cursor, then the actual markup below it, `<button class="button button1">Green</button>` and `<button class="button button2">Blue</button>`. The block renders live on the canvas behind the panel as you type. HTML and CSS run this way on any plan; a `<script>` tag needs Core or higher, so if nothing happens when you add one, check the plan before you assume a typo.

image.caption: The Code block's Content panel in HTML mode, with CSS button styles and markup on the left and the live-rendered Green and Blue buttons visible on the page behind it.

steps.heading: Preview on both device sizes before you trust it
steps.body: The block renders inline as you edit, which gives an immediate check, but that in-editor preview doesn't always match every screen size. Use the desktop and mobile preview icons in the top toolbar, since a button pair or embedded script that looks fine on desktop can overflow or misalign on a narrow mobile viewport. Save only after checking both. The Save button sits top left next to Exit, and until it's clicked, HTML changes exist only in the draft state.

steps.heading: When a block doesn't render
steps.body: A blank or broken block is usually a syntax error: an unclosed tag, a missing closing brace on a CSS rule, or a class name that doesn't match between the `<style>` block and the markup below it. Toggle Display Source Code on to see the raw text instead of the executed result, which makes a stray character easy to spot. If the block renders but looks wrong, check for a class name collision with Squarespace's own theme styles; renaming custom classes to something unlikely to exist elsewhere on the page, like a prefixed `.pmn-button1`, usually resolves it. And if a script simply does nothing, confirm the site is on Core or a higher plan before debugging further.

tables.title: When to reach for a Code block instead of a native block
rows: A link to another page or section
An RSS feed or a list of past posts
A custom button style, or a script with no native integration
tables.note: Native blocks inherit your site's fonts, spacing, and color palette automatically; a Code block has to be styled by hand to match.

troubleshooting.problem: The block shows blank or broken
troubleshooting.cause: Usually a syntax error: an unclosed tag, a missing closing brace on a CSS rule, or a class name that doesn't match between the <style> block and the markup below it.
troubleshooting.fix: Turn on Display Source Code to see the raw text rather than the rendered result, which makes a stray character easy to spot.

troubleshooting.cause: The site is on Squarespace's Basic plan, which supports HTML, Markdown, and CSS in Code blocks but not JavaScript execution or code injection.
troubleshooting.fix: Upgrade to Core or higher, or replace the script with a native block if one covers the same need.

troubleshooting.problem: The block renders but looks wrong
troubleshooting.cause: A custom class name collides with one Squarespace's own theme styles already use.
troubleshooting.fix: Rename the custom classes to something unlikely to exist elsewhere on the page, like a prefixed .pmn-button1.

faq.question: Do I need coding skills to add HTML to Squarespace?
faq.answer: Basic familiarity with HTML and CSS helps a lot, since the Code block is a plain text editor with no visual assistance, but simple embeds can often be added by pasting existing code from elsewhere.

faq.question: Can adding custom HTML break my Squarespace site?
faq.answer: A broken Code block typically only affects that block, not the whole page, but always check both desktop and mobile previews before saving, since layout issues are the most common problem.

faq.question: Is custom HTML available on all Squarespace plans?
faq.answer: HTML, Markdown, and CSS inside a Code block are available on every plan, including Basic. Running JavaScript in a Code block, or using site-wide code injection, needs the Core plan or higher.

faq.question: What are common reasons to add HTML to a Squarespace site?
faq.answer: Custom buttons with specific styling and embedding a script or widget with no native integration are the main cases. Check the Links and Integrations sections first, since many common needs already have a native block.

faq.question: Where exactly is the Code block located?
faq.answer: Click Edit on a page, then the plus icon to add a block. Code sits near the top of the panel under a "Code" heading, alongside Markdown and Embed.
